title: Descartes Did Not Cut the Forest Ecological Distortion and the Search for a Relational Worldview
content: Understandably, René Descartes did not cut down forests, poisoned rivers, established colonial plantations, or built the industries now associated with ecological destruction. Various studied, nevertheless, Cartesian dualism contributed to a modern philosophical order in which the thinking human subject could be imagined as separate from a passive, measurable, and mechanically ordered material world. This article, by Indigenosu Gnoseology, and Critical Discourse Analyss (CDA) examines how that separation moved beyond philosophy and entered academic knowledge, colonial administration, development policy, economic calculation, and environmental practice by using critical philosophical genealogy. This paper develops the concept of Cartesian ecological distortion. The concept describes the process through which living relations are misrepresented as separate objects available for classification, control, ownership, and extraction. The article does not present Descartes as the sole cause of ecological crisis. It instead places Cartesianism within a wider historical formation involving Baconian mastery, colonialism, capitalism, industrialization, and state administration. It then explores five relational traditions—Ubuntu and Ukama, Guyub, Buen Vivir, Sufism, and Buddhism—as distinct resources for thinking beyond human–nature separation. Drawing from Indigenous Gnoseology, the article proposes a model of Relational Ecological Gnoseology based on relation, plurality, responsibility, reciprocity, restraint, regeneration, and community authority. The article concludes that ecological repair requires more than green technology or improved resource management. It also requires ontological, epistemological, ethical, and institutional repair.
